title_original: Two Stolen Renoirs Worth $10M Recovered in France
excerpt_original: France's culture minister, Catherine Pégard, praised investigators for their speedy work.

blocks.text: Two Pierre-Auguste Renoir paintings stolen from a museum in the French Riviera last month have been recovered, local officials said. Six suspects were arrested.

The mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, where Renoir lived out his final days, described the news as “a source of immense joy and a great relief.” He added that the paintings were “part of our city’s history, our cultural heritage.”

Two thieves broke into the artist’s former home, the city’s Renoir Museum , early on September 8. They attempted to take four paintings before dropping two in the garden as they rushed to escape. The value of the two stolen works, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Young Woman at the Well (1886), was reported at a combined $10 million. Both belong to the Musée d’Orsay in Paris and were on loan.

The Marseille public prosecutor’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how the Renoir paintings were recovered. A press conference that would have given more details about the recovery was canceled so as not to interfere with the ongoing investigation.

France’s culture minister, Catherine Pégard , commended “the efficiency and determination” of the investigators in a post on social media. She also praised the “swift response” of local police, “from the moment the alarm was triggered,” as “remarkable.”

France has suffered a spate of museum heists in recent years. The highest-profile one occurred at the Louvre in Paris last October. Investigators uncovered various security failings that left the institution vulnerable to the shock $102 million theft, and the Louvre announced a $92 million master security plan .

Though Renoir continues to divide opinion , the Impressionist just broke box-office records at the National Gallery in London, with the museum selling over 22,000 tickets for its “Renoir and Love” exhibition, which is on view through January 31.
